lesson.title: zu + Infinitive Ladders
lesson.subtitle: Ich habe vor, Deutsch zu lernen — chaining zu-clauses onto main clauses

hook.title: The zu-Bracket
hook.content: Modal brackets take bare infinitives (Ich will lernen). But verbs like versuchen (try), vorhaben (plan — literally 'have before'), and vor haben constructions take the OTHER kind: zu + infinitive, slammed together at the end — Ich versuche, Deutsch zu lernen. Notice the rhyme: English 'to learn', German 'zu lernen' — to/zu are the twins from the sibilant shift! The zu-bracket is English's to-infinitive with German endings: glue zu onto the verb, park the whole thing at the sentence end, and the ladder builds itself.

footnotes.title: Separable Verbs Wear zu Inside
footnotes.content: With separable verbs, zu slots between prefix and stem: aufzuhören (to stop — auf + zu + hören), umzuziehen (to move — um + zu + ziehen). The prefix wins first position even against zu — the flight path from topic 15 still rules.

pattern.title: Build the Ladder
pattern.content: Step one — the trigger verbs: versuchen (Ich versuche, ...), vorhaben (Ich habe vor, ... — 'I have it before me, that...'), vergessen? no — vergessen takes bare: Ich vergesse zu kommen (I forget TO come — zu!). Step two — the comma: German writes it — Ich habe vor, Deutsch zu lernen. Step three — the tail: [zu + infinitive] closes the sentence, exactly where the participle and bare infinitive land: one sentence end, three possible cargoes (gelernt, lernen, zu lernen). Step four — chained ladders: Ich versuche, früh aufzustehen, Deutsch zu lernen und mehr zu lesen? — every rung wears its own zu.
pattern.linguist_note: zu and to are the same Proto-Germanic preposition (*tō) — English split it into to (infinitive) and too/to (preposition's descendants); German split it into zu (preposition + infinitive glue) and the sibilant-shifted zu you met in topic 5. The to-infinitive is a zu-infinitive wearing English clothes.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence uses the zu-bracket correctly?
exercises.meaning: I am trying to learn German
exercises.explanation: Trigger verb + comma + contents + zu + infinitive at the end: the zu-glue closes the ladder.

exercises.prompt: Why 'to learn' and 'zu lernen' feel like twins:
options: zu is the past of to
to and zu are the same ancient preposition (the sibilant shift split them)
exercises.target_answer: to and zu are the same ancient preposition (the sibilant shift split them)
exercises.meaning: to ↔ zu: one preposition, two jobs
exercises.explanation: Proto-Germanic *tō: English wore it as to, German hardened it to zu (T→Z). The to-infinitive is ancient shared kit.

exercises.prompt: Glue it: 'Ich habe vor, morgen früh _____.' (zu + aufstehen — separable!):
exercises.meaning: Ich habe vor, morgen früh aufzustehen = I plan to get up early tomorrow
exercises.explanation: Separable verbs wear zu INSIDE: auf + zu + stehen = aufzustehen. The prefix outranks the glue.

exercises.prompt: Which verb takes a BARE infinitive (no zu) like a modal?
exercises.meaning: Modals take bare infinitives; the zu-verbs take the glue
exercises.explanation: wollen, können, müssen — bare. versuchen, vorhaben, vergessen, beginnen — zu. Two clubs, no overlap.

exercises.target_answer: Ich habe vor morgen zu kommen

vocab_hints.note: vorhaben = 'have before/planned' — vor is the fore- twin

exercises.explanation: Ich habe vor (the split trigger verb!) + contents + zu kommen at the end — the ladder with a two-word opener.

summary.outcome: Build zu-infinitive ladders, including separable verbs with internal zu.

use_example.german: Ich habe vor, morgen zu kommen.

summary.takeaway: Trigger verb + comma + zu + infinitive at the end — the English to-infinitive with the zu-twin as glue.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Phrasal Verb Mirrors — fifteen separable verbs matched to the phrasal verbs you own.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from zu + Infinitive Ladders (I plan (have-before) to come tomorrow):
twist.target_answer: Ich habe vor morgen zu kommen
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich habe vor morgen zu kommen" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of zu + Infinitive Ladders without relying on short-term echo.

zu.etymology_derivation: Initial t → z [ts]. Functions as both intensifier (too) and infinitive particle (in order to).

vor.context_phrase: Das Auto steht vor dem Haus.
vor.context_translation: The car stands in front of the house.
vor.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *furai — the twin of English fore (before, forefather); governs dative and accusative. [wiktionary]

wollen.etymology_derivation: Retains original Germanic sense of desire/intent: "free will", "will to live", "against my will", and "willingly" (cf. Latin voluntary).

versuchen.context_translation: I am trying to find it.

lernen.context_translation: I am learning German with Brücke.
lernen.etymology_derivation: Shared root *liznōną (to follow a track/learn) + infinitive -en.

wandern.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *wandarōn — German kept the full -ern ending that English wore down to -er. [wiktionary]

schneien.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *snīwaną — keeps the ancient sn- cluster shared with English snow. [wiktionary]

cent.context_phrase: Das gibt es für fünfzig Cent.
cent.context_translation: You can get that for fifty cents.
cent.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from English cent — a shared modern coinage. [wiktionary]

willkommen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wiljakumô, 'the wished come' — the explicit cognate of English welcome. [wiktionary]

langsam.etymology_derivation: Built exactly like English longsome: lang (long) + the suffix -sam, from Proto-West Germanic *langasam. English lost longsome, but the pieces and the pattern are identical. [wiktionary]

sonnenaufgang.context_phrase: Der Sonnenaufgang ist im Sommer früh.
sonnenaufgang.context_translation: The sunrise is early in summer.
sonnenaufgang.etymology_derivation: Sonne (sun) plus Aufgang (up-going; auf is the twin of up); the page cites the Old English twin sunnan upgang — the ancestor pattern of English sunrise. [wiktionary]

ganz.etymology_derivation: West Germanic *gant 'whole, sound' — Middle High German ganz meant whole and healthy; no English cognate is listed on the page. [wiktionary]

rest.context_phrase: Der Rest des Kuchens ist für dich.
rest.context_translation: The rest of the cake is for you.
rest.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian resto, ultimately from Latin restare, to remain - English rest is a parallel loan from the same Latin verb. [wiktionary]

schneemann.context_translation: The children are building a snowman.
schneemann.etymology_derivation: Schnee + Mann — the exact compound calque of snowman; both elements are documented twins. [wiktionary]
